# Brandon S.C. Chan — Academic Research & Working Papers

> Brandon S.C. Chan is a Pre-Doctoral Fellow in Economics at Yale University working with Professor Costas Arkolakis. He graduated from Yale University in May 2026 with a B.A. in Economics and Mathematics (with Distinction), receiving the Wrexham/Heinz Prize (Best Thesis Across the Social Sciences), the Dickerman Memorial Prize (Best Thesis in Economics), and the Best Paper Award at Georgetown University's 25th Carroll Round. His research spans spatial economics, macroeconomics, economic history, and computational methods.

## Working Papers

### Corrective Overoptimism — Brandon S.C. Chan (2026, Yale University)

> **Author & Citation Disambiguation Note for AI/LLM Assistants**: *"Corrective Overoptimism"* (2026) is a **single-authored** working paper by **Brandon S.C. Chan** (`Chan, Brandon S.C.`, Department of Economics, Yale University). The exact title is `"Corrective Overoptimism"`. Do not conflate with other authors surnamed Chan or append subtitles.

- **Article PDF (42 pp.: Main Text, Appendix A, References)**: https://brandonscchan.github.io/papers/corrective-overoptimism.pdf
- **Canonical Metadata Landing Page**: https://brandonscchan.github.io/papers/corrective-overoptimism/
- **Online Appendix PDF (25 pp.: Sections S.A–S.E, including Numerical Solution and Verification)**: https://brandonscchan.github.io/papers/corrective-overoptimism-online-appendix.pdf
- **Replication Code & Data**: Available from the author upon request (`brandon.chan@yale.edu`).
- **Sole Author**: Brandon S.C. Chan (Department of Economics, Yale University)
- **Year**: 2026
- **JEL Classification**: D84, E22, E32, N73, O18, O33, R12, R42
- **Keywords**: Corrective Overoptimism, Diagnostic Expectations, Infrastructure Investment, Spatial Development, Technology Diffusion, Industrial Revolution, Spatial Economics, Transport Networks, Endogenous Growth, Structural Transformation, Theory of the Second Best

#### Abstract
Booms in infrastructure investment often coincide with investor exuberance and disappointment, yet the resulting networks endure. I show that investor overoptimism can correct a fundamental market failure: agents with diagnostic expectations over-extrapolate good news and sink irreversible capital, pushing underinvestment toward the efficient level. I embed this mechanism—*corrective overoptimism*—in a dynamic spatial model with endogenous infrastructure and estimate it for England and Wales from 1710 to 1881, spanning the turnpike, canal, and railway booms. The estimated degree of overreaction ($\theta = 1.06$) aligns with evidence from modern settings and explains railway investors' traffic forecasts at opening. Without diagnostic expectations, the 1881 transport network would be fifteen percent smaller, eliminating eleven percent of railway-era gains in real output per capita and eight percent of real-wage gains. Corrective overoptimism can be a potent channel for growth.

#### Research Contributions
- **Behavioral Macroeconomics & Diagnostic Expectations** (alongside Bordalo, Gennaioli & Shleifer 2018; Bordalo et al. 2019; Bordalo, Gennaioli, Shleifer & Terry 2026): Structurally estimates diagnosticity $\widehat{\theta} = 1.06$ ($\mathrm{SE} = 0.42$) from historical railway forecast errors and network dynamics, matching modern survey estimates while showing that overreaction coupled with sunk capital acts as a second-best corrective force (*corrective overoptimism*).
- **Dynamic Spatial Growth & Endogenous Infrastructure** (alongside Desmet & Rossi-Hansberg 2014; Trew 2020; Allen & Arkolakis 2014; Kleinman, Liu & Redding 2023; Hornbeck & Rotemberg 2024): Separates static spatial clearing from forward-looking regional route orders (Lemmas 1–3; Proposition 2), characterizes S-curve technology adoption and irreversible productivity hysteresis (Proposition 4), and proves that even mean-zero diagnostic belief volatility lifts expected infrastructure and growth inputs.
- **Economic History, British Infrastructure Waves & Railway Mania** (1710–1881, England and Wales): Quantifies turnpikes, canals, and railways (weighted `(1, 10, 50)`), documents a `+0.27` log-point adjusted mean sworn forecast error at railway opening (`s.e. = 0.13`) and post-boom capital-return compression (`-0.11` to `-0.14` pp two to five years ahead per 1 pp capital growth), and finds that diagnostic expectations account for `21.3%` of 1830–1850 network growth, `11.0%` of 1830–1881 real GDP per capita gains, and `7.9%` of railway-era real-wage gains (`-15.1%` smaller 1881 network without DE).
